title: Common Sass Errors
learning_outcomes: Explain common sass errors and connect it to at least two of its syllabus subtopics.
Apply common sass errors in a small SCSS example and predict the resulting CSS or compiler behavior.
Inspect the output, diagnose one plausible mistake, and state a relevant limitation or best practice.

content.intro: This lesson turns **Common Sass Errors** into a practical, inspectable step. You will connect syntax and parsing errors with undefined variables, then check what Dart Sass emits instead of relying on the SCSS source alone.
content.why_it_matters: A stylesheet is correct only when it compiles and behaves correctly in the target browser and interface. Keep the source, compiler diagnostics, generated CSS, and rendered page available while debugging.

content_blocks.title: The mental model
content_blocks.text: Use reproducible checks: compile the required entrypoints, inspect emitted selectors, test keyboard focus and reduced motion where relevant, and verify supported browser features independently of Sass syntax.

items.title: Syntax and parsing errors
items.text: Reproduce the issue with the smallest entrypoint, read the first relevant diagnostic, fix the source rather than the generated file, and recompile to verify the correction.

items.title: Undefined variables
items.text: Choose the variable scope and name for the decision it represents. Test default and overridden values so a new configuration does not silently change unrelated components.

items.title: Missing mixins or functions
items.text: Make the mixin contract explicit: name each option, select safe defaults, and show what declarations or nested rules it emits when included.

items.title: Module-resolution errors
items.text: Show where the member is defined and how consumers reach it. Namespaced `@use` is the modern default; `@forward` exposes a curated API, and legacy `@import` is deprecated.

items.title: Type and unit errors
items.text: Check the type and unit of each operand and decide whether the calculation belongs in Sass at build time or in CSS at browser runtime.

items.title: Invalid function arguments
items.text: Make the mixin contract explicit: name each option, select safe defaults, and show what declarations or nested rules it emits when included.

items.title: Understanding compiler stack traces
items.text: Trace the source rule to its emitted CSS and inspect the output file. Treat the browser-facing CSS, not the SCSS source, as the final artifact.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with the smallest source file that demonstrates common sass errors. 2. State what should change and what should stay the same. 3. Compile the entrypoint with Dart Sass, or use the stated command if this lesson is about the toolchain. 4. Compare the resulting CSS or diagnostic with the expected result, then change one input and repeat.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Common Sass Errors
content_blocks.expected_output: Compilation fails with an undefined-variable diagnostic. Fix the source reference, then compile again.
content_blocks.execution_note: This course example is a Sass/SCSS or tooling example. CodeLeaf’s current in-browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; compile Sass locally with Dart Sass. Do not treat the browser preview as a Sass compiler.

content_blocks.title: Modern Sass note
content_blocks.text: Use Dart Sass for new work. Prefer @use / @forward and namespaced sass: built-in modules. Sass compiles to CSS; browser-native CSS features still run in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Audit a small stylesheet for common sass errors. Save the original source and compiled CSS, make one deliberate change, recompile, and write down the evidence that the change is correct and safe.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Do not edit generated CSS when you intend to change source behavior. Edit the SCSS entrypoint or its module, compile again, and compare the generated output.

task: Audit a small stylesheet for common sass errors. Save the original source and compiled CSS, make one deliberate change, recompile, and write down the evidence that the change is correct and safe.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example includes the intended Sass construct and a clear input.
The expected output or tool result is documented and consistent with the source.
The work is reproducible and includes one limitation, test, or troubleshooting note.
hints: Reduce the example to one source file and one entrypoint before adding more abstractions.
Read the first compiler diagnostic and confirm you are editing the Sass source, not only generated CSS.
Compile and inspect the emitted CSS; compare exact selectors, values, and at-rules with your expectation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming SCSS runs directly in the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Browsers consume CSS, not Sass syntax.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with Dart Sass and load the resulting .css file in the HTML page.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting source readability without inspecting generated output.
common_mistakes.why: Nesting, mixins, loops, and extension can emit unexpected selectors or more CSS than intended.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile a small example and inspect the CSS output or browser computed styles.
